what_its_for: Vedolizumab is used to treat adults with moderate to severe Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis when other treatments have not worked well enough. It helps calm the inflammation in your gut by blocking certain immune cells from entering the lining of your intestines.
how_to_take: Vedolizumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein, or as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection. The IV infusion is given by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or infusion center and takes about 30 minutes. The under-the-skin injection can be given by a healthcare provider or, after proper training, by yourself at home. Rotate injection sites (abdomen, thigh) and never inject into skin that is bruised, tender, red, or hard.
dosing: For IV infusions: You will receive a dose at Week 0, Week 2, and Week 6 to start. After that, you will receive a dose every 8 weeks to maintain your treatment. For under-the-skin injections: After your first two IV infusions (at Week 0 and Week 2), your doctor may switch you to weekly injections of 108 mg starting at Week 6. Always follow the exact schedule your doctor gives you.
missed_dose: If you miss an IV infusion or a scheduled injection, contact your doctor as soon as possible to reschedule. Do not try to give yourself two doses at the same time to make up for a missed dose. Your doctor may need to restart your dosing schedule if too much time has passed.
storage: IV vials: Store in a refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze or shake the vials. Keep them in their original packaging to protect from light. Pre-filled pens or syringes for injection: Also store in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze. If needed, you may keep a pen or syringe at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to 7 days, but use it within that time or throw it away. Keep all forms out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid live vaccines (such as live flu vaccine, shingles vaccine Zostavax, yellow fever vaccine) while taking vedolizumab, as it may make them less effective or cause infection. Talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines. Avoid close contact with people who have active infections. Do not start taking vedolizumab if you currently have an active infection. Avoid stopping your medication without talking to your doctor first, even if you are feeling better.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: signs of a serious allergic reaction such as hives, itching, rash, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing, chest tightness, or dizziness during or after your infusion; signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, muscle aches, cough, shortness of breath, blood in urine, burning with urination, or a wound that will not heal; new or worsening numbness, tingling, weakness, vision problems, memory problems, or confusion, which could be signs of a rare but serious brain infection called PML; severe stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits that concern you; liver problems such as yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe fatigue.
when_it_works: Vedolizumab does not work overnight. Some patients begin to notice improvement in their symptoms within 6 to 14 weeks, but it may take up to 6 months or longer to feel the full benefit. It is very important to keep all your appointments and not stop treatment early, even if you do not feel different right away. Talk to your doctor if you have questions about how well the medication is working for you.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Vedolizumab can cross the placenta, especially in the last three months of pregnancy, and may affect the immune system of an unborn baby. If you received vedolizumab during pregnancy, your baby should not receive live vaccines for at least 6 months after birth. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits. Elderly patients: No dose adjustment is needed for older adults, but your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver disease: No special dose changes are required, but tell your doctor about any kidney or liver problems you have.
